title: Inequality
text:
Measures of Economics Inequality
Inequality, in economics, usually refers to either income and/or wealth inequality. That is, economic inequality, broadly speaking, is the unequal distribution of income (earnings) or wealth (net worth or savings) between individuals, groups, populations, social classes, or countries.
For example, on a global level, income inequality is extreme by any measure, with the richest 1 percent of people in the world receiving as much as the bottom 56 percent in the early 21st century. Within the United States, income inequality is much greater than in most other developed countries. In 2014, the richest 1 percent received 22 percent of total income, and the top 10 percent of U.S. households received about 60 percent of total income.


Four criteria for Inequality Measurement

Anonymity principle
Population principle
Relative income principle
The Dalton principle

A quick survey of the literature presents various measures of economic inequality:

Ratio measures,compare how much people at one level of the income distribution have compared to people at another. For instance, the 20:20 ratio compares how much richer the top 20% of people are, compared to the bottom 20%.
The Palma ratio is the ratio of the income share of the top 10% to that of the bottom 40%.

However, the most popular measure of inequality are:

Lorenz Curve
Gini Coefficient

title: Why Prisoners Learn Faster Than College Students
text:
Why Prisoners Learn Faster Than College Students
Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oBHzmFFNkW4
The YouTube source describe several key psychological and environmental principles that allow for accelerated learning, often observed in prison environments:
The Dopamine Detox Effect In prison, the total absence of internet, smartphones, and “cheap dopamine” sources like TikTok or Netflix forces a cognitive shift. While the average professional is interrupted every three minutes—and a study from the University of California shows it takes 23 minutes to fully refocus after just one interruption—prisoners engage in “deep work,” which is sustained, distraction-free concentration. This environment allows the brain to literally rewire its attention span, eventually making dense, complex texts enjoyable to read because the brain’s focus is restored.
Life or Death Learning Prisoners often study to survive rather than to earn a grade; for instance, many study law to fight their own cases because they lack effective legal counsel. This creates “desirable difficulty,” a psychological state where the high stakes cause the brain to flag information as critical and encode it permanently. A notable example is Malcolm X, who hand-copied the entire dictionary word-for-word because his inability to write a coherent letter was a source of personal shame, driving him to rebuild his intellect from the ground up.
The Scarcity Advantage While unlimited resources often lead to the “Google Effect”—where the brain refuses to store information it knows it can search for later—scarcity forces extreme depth of learning. Prisoners may have a maximum of three books, leading them to read each one ten times, analyze sentence structures, and internalize every detail. Because they cannot rely on external storage or “copy-paste” functionality, the knowledge is forced to live in their heads rather than on a device, making the information stick.
Applying These Principles to Your Learning System The sources suggest applying these high-intensity methods to your own life:
- The Dopamine Detox Checklist: Systematically remove digital distractions to restore your brain’s ability to focus on “boring” but important material.
- The Stakes Planner: Artificial or real consequences should be established so your brain views the material as critical for survival or success, rather than optional.
- The Three Source Rule: Limit your study materials to just three high-quality sources at a time to force deep mastery and repetition instead of surface-level skimming across infinite resources.
- Internalization over Externalization: Move away from relying solely on AI or digital note-taking; focus on memorizing and internalizing insights to ensure they are truly learned.

title: JB2
text:
CORE Econ
In the context of Jupyter Book 2 (MyST), if you are looking to replicate the style of the famous CORE Econ (Curriculum Open-access Resources in Economics) textbooks, you are in luck. CORE was one of the primary inspirations for the development of MyST Markdown and the new CLI.
While there isn’t a single “button” for a CORE template, you can achieve that specific look by configuring the book-theme in your myst.yml.


1. The “CORE” Configuration
The CORE style is defined by a clean sidebar, specific margin usage (sidenotes), and structured theorem/definition boxes. Add these to your site section:
site:
  template: book-theme
  options:
    # CORE often uses a "fixed" sidebar and a clean top nav
    hide_toc_from_sidebar: false
    # Enable sidenotes for that classic academic margin look
    sidenotes: true
    margin_references: true



2. Emulating CORE Features
CORE books rely heavily on specific components. Here is how you replicate them in JB2:

A. The “Leibniz” (Calculus/Math blocks)
CORE uses “Leibniz” popups for mathematical derivations. In JB2, you use the dropdown or proof directives:
::::{important} Leibniz: The Multiplier Effect
:dropdown:
In this section, we derive the multiplier...
$$
k = \frac{1}{1 - c_1}
$$
::::


B. Definitions in the Margin
CORE puts key terms in the margin. In JB2, use the {margin} directive:
:::{margin}
**Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)**: The trade-off that a person is willing to make between two goods.
:::
While the consumer moves along the indifference curve...




3. CSS for the “CORE” Look
To get the exact fonts and colors (like the specific CORE green/blue), you can add a custom CSS file.

Create a file named custom.css.
Link it in your myst.yml:

site:
  template: book-theme
  css: custom.css
Common CORE Colors:
:root {
  --pst-color-primary: #007d8a; /* CORE-style teal */
  --pst-color-info: #2d5973;
}



4. Project Structure (The “Units” approach)
CORE books are organized into “Units” rather than chapters. Reflect this in your toc:
site:
  toc:
    - file: intro.md
    - title: Unit 1 - The Capitalist Revolution
      sections:
        - file: unit_01/01_intro.md
        - file: unit_01/02_inequality.ipynb


Is there a pre-built theme?
There is an ongoing effort by the Executuable Books Project and Curvenote (who build MyST) to support these open-curriculum styles natively. Since you are using JB2, keep an eye on the curvenote template as an alternative to book-theme if you want a more “Journal/Scientific” look.

Data Structure in R
There are four main types of data structures in R:

Vectors
Matrix
Data.frame
Lists


Vectors
Vectors are the basic unit for data storage in R. Vectors can store one or more values of the same type (numeric or character strings).
# Vector of strings
x <- c("Germany", "Argentina", "Netherlands")
# Replacing the second element of the vector
x[2] <- NA
x  # [1] "Germany"    NA           "Netherlands"
x[!is.na(x)]  # [1] "Germany"    "Netherlands"


Vector Classes
# character vectors
x <- c("Germany", "Argentina", "Netherlands")
class(x)  # [1] "character"

x <- c(1.1, 2.5)
class(x)  # [1] "numeric"

x <- 1:4
class(x)  # [1] "integer"

x <- x > 2
class(x)  # [1] "logical"


Matrices
There are many ways to define a matrix.
matrix(1:6, ncol=2)
#      [,1] [,2]
# [1,]    1    4
# [2,]    2    5
# [3,]    3    6

matrix(1:6, nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6

r1 = c(1,2)
r2 = c(3,4)
A = rbind(r1, r2)
A
#    [,1] [,2]
# r1    1    2
# r2    3    4

t(A)  # transpose
#    r1 r2
# [1,] 1  3
# [2,] 2  4

det(A)  # determinant, [1] -2

solve(A)  # inverse
#     r1   r2
# [1,] -2  1.0
# [2,] 1.5 -0.5

r1 = c(1,-2)
r2 = c(0,1)
B = rbind(r1, r2)

A+B  # matrix addition
A%*%B  # matrix multiplication


Data Frames
Think of data frames as specialized type of lists that can do more than usual matrices.
df <- data.frame(
  patientID = c("001", "002", "003"),
  treatment = c("drug", "placebo", "drug"),
  age = c(20, 30, 24)
)

df
#   patientID treatment age
# 1       001      drug  20
# 2       002   placebo  30
# 3       003      drug  24

subset(df, treatment == "drug")
#   patientID treatment age
# 1       001      drug  20
# 3       003      drug  24


Lists
Lists are powerful and versatile data structures. You can store any data structure in lists, even lists.
my.list <- list(
  fruits = c("oranges", "bananas", "apples"),
  mat = matrix(1:10, nrow=2)
)

my.list
# $fruits
# [1] "oranges" "bananas" "apples"
#
# $mat
#      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
# [1,]    1    3    5    7    9
# [2,]    2    4    6    8   10

Importing Data
It is easy to import data into R. Simply invoke import and export R functions, which exist for many formats including:

text or ASCII files
proprietary formats (e.g. SAS, Stata, SPSS, Excel, etc)
databases (Oracle, MySQL, couchDB, SQLite, etc)
R data and S
XML, HTML tables and many more


Reading ASCII/Text files
A quick way to access a csv file is:
read.csv(file.choose(), header=TRUE)
The most common R command to import data from text/csv datafiles is read.table and read.csv, e.g.:
URL <- "https:// ... /scorer2014.csv"
scorer <- read.table(URL, sep='', header=TRUE)
scorer$name
# [1] Rodriguez Muller Neymer Messi
# Levels: Messi Muller Neymer Rodriguez
class(scorer)  # [1] "data.frame"
To check your current directory type getwd(), which you can change, for example, by setwd("C:/Users/YY/Documents/R").


Reading Foreign Files
Use haven for SPSS and Stata – it’s actively maintained, handles modern versions, and integrates well with tidyverse workflows.
install.packages("haven")    # Install if needed
library(haven)

# Read SPSS file
mydata <- read_sav("myfile.sav")

# Read Stata data file
mydata <- read_dta("mydata.dta")

The readxl package is now the standard way to import Excel files into R, replacing older approaches like gdata::read.xls or xlsx.
# Read a data frame to Excel

install.packages("readxl")    # Install if needed
library(readxl)
mydata <- read_excel("mydata.xlsx", sheet = 1)

# Write a data frame to Excel

install.packages("writexl")
library(writexl)
write_xlsx(mydata, "output.xlsx")
The more modern alternative is openxlsx:
install.packages("openxlsx")   # Install if needed

library(openxlsx)
mydata <- read.xlsx("mydata.xlsx", sheet = 1)   # Read Excel file

# Write a data frame to Excel
write.xlsx(mydata, file = "output.xlsx", sheetName = "Sheet1", overwrite = TRUE)


Exporting Data
To save as R data:
save(scorer, file="scorer2014.Rda")
load("scorer2014.Rda")  # to reload your saved data
If you want to export your data to a csv file you may use write.csv or to a text file use write.table:
write.csv(mydata, "scorer2014.csv")
write.table(mydata, file="scorer2014.csv", sep = ',')
To export data into other formats (SPSS, Stata) use haven package:
# Write to SPSS (.sav)
write_sav(mydata, "output.sav") 

# Write to Stata (.dta)

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
# How do we avoid the predictions of Wall-E?


Strategic Insight: The professional landscape has shifted from search engines to answer engines. In a world where Large Language Models (LLMs) generate dazzling responses on command, information is no longer a competitive advantage—it is a commodity.
For decades, the dominant economic narrative was the knowledge economy. Those who possessed expertise or could access information faster than others held a meaningful advantage. Search engines reinforced this system by rewarding individuals who knew where to look and how to interpret the results.
But something fundamental has changed.
Artificial intelligence has transformed search engines into answer engines. Today, anyone can ask a complex question and receive a polished explanation in seconds. Knowledge that once required years of study or professional experience is now widely accessible.
When answers become cheap, something else becomes valuable.
For twenty years, since the publication of A Whole New Mind, observers of technological change have tracked the evolution of cognitive labor. The conclusion is increasingly clear: when information becomes abundant, human curiosity and ways of thinking become the ultimate competitive advantage.
We have entered what might be called the Allocation Economy.
In this new environment, your value is no longer determined primarily by what you know. Instead, it depends on how effectively you orchestrate intelligence—your own, other people’s, and increasingly that of machines.
To remain irreplaceable in this world, professionals must cultivate six core human capabilities:
Questioning, Taste, Iteration, Composition, Allocation, and Integrity.
These skills represent the emerging architecture of human advantage.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Scale of Effort
True iteration often requires far more work than people initially expect.
Many creative and technical achievements are the result of thousands of small improvements rather than a single breakthrough moment.

James Dyson built more than 5,000 prototypes before perfecting the cyclone vacuum cleaner that made his company successful. Each prototype revealed a flaw that could only be discovered through experimentation.
Willem de Kooning, one of the leading painters of abstract expressionism, sometimes worked on a single canvas for two years, repeatedly scraping off paint and starting again until the composition felt right.
Thomas Edison reportedly tested thousands of filament materials before arriving at a workable light bulb design.

These examples illustrate a common pattern: excellence is rarely instantaneous.
Iteration is not merely repetition. Each cycle incorporates new insight. Every revision moves the work closer to its intended form.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Version 0.8 Rule
A common obstacle to iteration is perfectionism.
Many people delay sharing their work because they believe it must be completely finished before others see it. This instinct often slows progress and prevents useful feedback.
The Version 0.8 Rule offers an alternative approach:
Ship your work when it is roughly 80 percent complete.
At this stage, the core idea is visible, but there is still room for improvement. Releasing work early allows others to react, critique, and suggest improvements.
This feedback becomes part of the next iteration cycle.
The result is a continuous process of improvement rather than a long period of isolated perfectionism.
In many fields—from software development to academic writing—progress depends on rapid cycles of iteration rather than waiting for a perfect first version.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
Tactical Habits for Performance
Iteration is not just a philosophy; it is a set of habits.
Several simple practices make the process more effective.

1. The Shitty First Draft Principle
The most important barrier to creative work is often getting started.
Writer Anne Lamott popularized the idea of the “shitty first draft.” The goal of the first draft is not quality. Its purpose is simply to exist.
Once something exists, it can be improved.
Lowering the standard for the first attempt reduces resistance and allows the iteration process to begin.


2. The One Week Rule
Distance improves judgment.
After completing a draft or prototype, leave it alone for several days before revising. When you return with fresh eyes, weaknesses that were previously invisible become obvious.
This time gap allows your brain to shift from creator mode to editor mode, making it easier to identify flaws and opportunities for improvement.


3. Refine vs Generate
Artificial intelligence is extremely effective at generating options.
Humans are far better at refining them.
A productive workflow often looks like this:

Use AI to generate a wide range of possibilities.
Select the most promising option.
Improve structure, clarity, and nuance through human editing.
Repeat the process until the work reaches the desired standard.

In other words:
AI produces quantity.
Humans create quality.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Rule of Three
One of the most reliable principles of effective composition is the Rule of Three.
Ideas organized into three parts tend to be easier to understand and remember than longer lists. Human cognition naturally gravitates toward patterns of three because they create balance and rhythm.
Consider common examples:

beginning, middle, end

past, present, future

problem, analysis, solution

Many memorable speeches and stories follow this structure. The Rule of Three creates a sense of progression that helps audiences follow complex ideas.
For example, a presentation about innovation might naturally organize itself into:

The challenge

The insight

The solution

This structure transforms scattered information into a clear narrative arc.

Visual Composition Drills
Composition is not limited to writing or speaking. It is also a visual skill.
Simple exercises can help train the mind to recognize how elements interact within a frame.

The Camera Grid
Most smartphone cameras allow you to enable a 3×3 grid.
This grid illustrates the Rule of Thirds, a classic composition principle in photography and visual design. Instead of placing subjects in the center, strong images often position key elements along the intersecting grid lines.
This creates visual tension and balance.


The Movie Pause Game
Another exercise is to pause a visually striking film during a quiet scene and analyze how the frame is constructed.
Ask yourself:

Where are the characters positioned?
What lines in the environment guide the viewer’s eye?
How does lighting emphasize certain elements?

Directors carefully compose each shot to guide attention and create emotional impact. Studying these techniques trains your ability to see relationships rather than isolated objects.
Over time, this awareness improves not only visual design but also writing, presentations, and strategic thinking.
Composition is the skill that turns information into meaning.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Time as Talent Audit
To improve allocation skills, conduct a time-as-talent audit.
Review your calendar from the past two weeks and identify tasks that did not require your unique strengths.
Ask yourself three questions:

Could a tool have done this?
Could another person have handled this?
Did this task truly require my judgment?

Circle any activity that could have been delegated or automated.
Those hours represent misallocated talent.
The next step is to redesign your workflow so that your time is invested in tasks that require human insight—creative thinking, strategy, relationship building, and decision-making.
Allocation is the ability to direct intelligence where it creates the most value.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Washington Post Test
A simple technique for maintaining ethical clarity is the Washington Post Test.
Before taking an action, ask:
Would I be comfortable if this decision appeared on the front page of a major newspaper?
If the answer is no, it is a signal to pause and reconsider.
This question forces transparency into decision-making. It removes the protective illusion that questionable choices will remain hidden.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
The Integrity Inversion
Another useful technique is the Integrity Inversion.
Reverse the situation and ask:
If someone did this to me or someone I care about, would it feel fair?
This mental reversal cuts through rationalization and forces you to consider the impact of your decision on others.
It transforms ethical reflection from an abstract principle into a practical test.

title: Late-Stage Capitalism
text:
Late-stage Capitalism
This post is based on a talk I gave at the IDEAs Conference on Bangkok



What is late stage capitalism?
Late-stage capitalism, a term often used in critical discourse, refers to the contemporary phase of capitalism characterized by specific economic, social, and technological features. In the context of today’s fast-paced, technologically driven situation within late capitalism, several characteristics stand out:
Rapid Technological Advancements: Late capitalism is marked by unprecedented technological innovation and advancements. The rapid development of information technology, artificial intelligence, automation, and digital communication has transformed industries, economies, and daily life.
Globalization: The global interconnectedness of markets, economies, and cultures is a defining feature of late capitalism. Companies operate on a global scale, leading to complex networks of production, distribution, and consumption that transcend national borders.
Digitalization of Economy: The economy (local and global) is becoming increasingly digital, with online platforms, e-commerce, and digital services playing a central role. This has led to new business models, changes in consumer behavior, and the emergence of digital platforms as key economic actors.
Financialization: There is an increased dominance of financial markets and financial institutions in shaping economic activities. Speculation, financial instruments, and the prioritization of shareholder value have become central aspects of economic decision-making. Financial instruments and speculation often have a profound impact on various economic sectors.
Flexible Labor Markets: Late capitalism is characterized by a shift towards flexible labor arrangements, including gig work and temporary employment. Job insecurity, precarious employment, and a focus on short-term profits are prevalent in this economic landscape.
Consumer Culture: Consumption plays a central role in late capitalism. Advertising and marketing techniques are sophisticated, contributing to a culture of constant consumption and a desire for the latest products and experiences.
Commodification of Everyday Life: Late capitalism tends to commodify various aspects of life, turning even social interactions, cultural products, and personal experiences into marketable entities.
Surveillance Capitalism: The widespread collection and analysis of personal data have become integral to many business models. Companies (and in some cases governments) leverage user data for targeted advertising/propaganda, personalization, and other purposes, raising concerns about privacy and surveillance.
Inequality: Late capitalism is associated with growing income and wealth inequality. The benefits of economic growth are often concentrated among a small elite, leading to social and economic disparities.
Acceleration of Time: The pace of life in late capitalism is often described as accelerated. Rapid communication, instant access to information, and the expectation of quick results contribute to a sense of urgency and constant activity.
Crisis as Normalcy: Periodic economic crises are considered normal within late capitalism. Financial downturns and recessions are seen as inherent features of the system, leading to a cycle of boom and bust.
Environmental Challenges: The pursuit of profit often comes at the expense of environmental sustainability. Late capitalism is associated with environmental degradation, resource depletion, and climate change, prompting concerns about the long-term viability of current economic practices.
These characteristics contribute to a complex and dynamic socio-economic environment, prompting ongoing discussions and critiques about the nature of contemporary capitalism and its impact on society.


The Issue

Internet and social media: We are constantly exposed to the .00001% of top performers (good-looking people, at amazing locations, doing awesome things, 24/7/365 … Twitter - OMG Apocalypse! … Facebook - everyone has amazing lives, families, etc.)


“Everyone in their Instagram post wants you to believe that the key to a good life is a nicer job, or a faster car, a prettier girlfriend or a selfie on a beach.”


We seem to be living on a hedonic treadmill: “More, more, more!”
The “can-do” society: “You can be whatever you want to be!” leads to “entitlement” (a delusional belief to move you from reality, i.e., life is tough!)
The Digital Panopticon: Today, the entire globe is developing into a panopticon. Google and social networks, which present themselves as spaces of freedom, are assuming panoptic forms. Today, surveillance is not occurring as an attack on freedom, as is normally assumed. Instead, people are voluntarily surrendering to the panoptic gaze. They deliberately collaborate in the digital panopticon by denuding and exhibiting themselves. The prisoner of the digital panopticon is a perpetrator and a victim at the same time. Herein lies the dialectic of freedom: freedom turns out to be a form of control.



Freedom turns out to be a form of control.




Positive vs Negative Power
The negative power of prohibition and limitation in disciplinary societies vs the positive power of freedom and achievement in neoliberal societies.
The positivity of can is much more effective than the negativity of should. Therefore, the social unconscious switches from should to can.
Positive power is more effective and insidious, as it turns people into self-exploiting narcissists who are constantly working on themselves as personal projects


The Achievement Society

Psychopolitics is an extension of Foucault’s biopolitics. You don’t need a gun to people’s heads because in the pursuit of endlessly maximizing their abilities, they’ll spend the rest of their lives going crazy about never being good enough, never doing enough, never being efficient enough. If there’s ever a moment where they’re not spending their time being as productive as they possibly could towards making themselves more valuable, they will actually feel bad about it.



Loss of other / Terror of the Same

Consequences of this positive power include the loss of the other, the terror of the same, the crisis of connection and love, and the rise of depression and anxiety.
Authenticity and diversity: Authenticity is an ad campaign of neoliberalism. It’s a self-absorbed nightmare.
Loss of other: People avoid encountering differences and negativity.
Terror of the same: Everything becomes the same and meaningless.
Crisis of connection (and love)
Technology and social media isolate people
Information vs knowledge, thinking and calculating: The importance of contemplation and depth: Meaning, knowledge, truth, are things that only come when you contemplate how the present moment connects to the past and the future.



The psycho-politics of neoliberalism

Auto-exploitation
Commodification of oneself
Tendency towards narcissim: The narcissistic individual is not the cause of the world being more narcissistic. The ethos of the world (late-capitalism) makes narcissism an extremely common lane for people to fall into.
Rise of depression, anxiety, mental illness

title: A Practical Guide to the Six Skills AI Cannot Replace
text:
Simple Example
Imagine a factory machine has stopped working.

Why did the machine stop? Because the circuit breaker tripped.
Why did the circuit breaker trip? Because the motor was overloaded.
Why was the motor overloaded? Because the bearing was not properly lubricated.
Why was the bearing not lubricated? Because the lubrication schedule was not followed.
Why was the schedule not followed? Because the maintenance procedure was never clearly documented.

At first glance, the problem appeared to be a mechanical failure. But the Five Whys reveal that the real cause is a management or process problem.
Example: Using AI to find a contractor for a website redesign.

Why do the AI recommendations feel wrong?
None of them seem like a good fit.
Why are they not a fit?
Their proposals vary widely.
Why are the proposals inconsistent?
Contractors are making different assumptions about the project.
Why are they making assumptions?
The scope and success criteria were never clearly defined.
Why is there no clear criteria?
The internal team never agreed on what success looks like.

Result: The real problem is internal misalignment, not the contractor list.
Artificial intelligence can generate answers.
Humans must determine whether the question itself is correct.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
Building Your “Hall of Fame”
Building your “Hall of Fame” is a practical method for developing taste and discernment. Instead of relying on vague intuition about what “good” work looks like, you deliberately collect and study examples of excellence in your field. Over time, this curated collection becomes a reference system that sharpens your judgment.
In essence, a Hall of Fame is a personal archive of the best ideas, designs, writing, arguments, or solutions you encounter—the things that immediately stand out as unusually effective, elegant, or insightful.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
section: Why Build a Hall of Fame?
text:
Why Build a Hall of Fame?
In the age of AI, machines can generate a huge volume of content quickly. The challenge is no longer producing ideas but recognizing which ones are actually good. This is where human taste becomes valuable.
A Hall of Fame helps train this ability by exposing you repeatedly to examples of high-quality work. By studying them closely, you begin to recognize patterns of excellence.
Over time, this process improves your ability to:

distinguish strong ideas from mediocre ones

recognize effective structure and design

refine AI-generated output

raise your personal standards

In other words, it turns taste into a deliberate practice rather than a vague feeling.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
How to Build One
Building a Hall of Fame is simple but requires consistency.

1. Capture Exceptional Examples
Whenever you encounter something that stands out—an insightful paragraph, a clever chart, an elegant explanation, a striking design—save it.
This could include:

a beautifully written article

a clear explanation of a complex idea

a powerful presentation slide

an elegant data visualization

a memorable product design

a clever piece of code

The key question is:
“Does this make my brain light up?”
If yes, it belongs in your Hall of Fame.



2. Store It in One Place
Your collection should live somewhere you can easily revisit. Possible options include:

Notion

Obsidian

a simple notes folder

a Dropbox archive

a physical notebook

Organization can be simple. Categories might include:

Writing

Design

Explanations

Data visualization

Strategy

Teaching




3. Study the Patterns
The most important step is not just collecting examples but analyzing them.
Ask questions such as:

Why does this work so well?
What structure makes the argument clear?
What makes the visual design effective?
What is omitted as much as what is included?

Sometimes the brilliance lies in negative space—what the creator chose not to include.

For example, the famous FedEx logo contains a hidden arrow between the “E” and “x.” Once you see it, you cannot unsee it. That subtle design choice communicates motion and direction without using additional graphics.
This type of observation trains your eye for quality.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
How It Improves Your Work
Over time, your Hall of Fame becomes a mental reference library. When you write, design, or build something, you unconsciously draw upon these stored examples.
Instead of asking:

“What should I do?”

your mind asks:

“What do the best examples look like?”

This dramatically improves the quality of your decisions.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
section: Why It Matters in the AI Era
text:
Why It Matters in the AI Era
AI systems can generate enormous quantities of content. But they cannot reliably judge quality in the same way humans can.
A strong Hall of Fame allows you to:

quickly evaluate AI-generated output

identify promising ideas among many weak ones

refine raw material into something meaningful

In other words, the machine produces quantity, while your Hall of Fame helps you recognize quality.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
text:
Simple Summary
Building a Hall of Fame means:

Collecting examples of excellence

Studying why they work

Using them as a reference for your own standards

Over time, it becomes a powerful tool for sharpening taste, judgment, and creativity—skills that remain deeply human even as artificial intelligence grows more capable.

title: Human Advantage in the Era of AI
section: Why Iteration Matters in the AI Era
text:

Tasks that once took hours—drafting text, producing visual variations, or brainstorming ideas—can now be completed in seconds. But this abundance creates a new challenge: the real skill is no longer producing ideas, but improving them.
The risk is that people stop too early.
When an AI system produces a polished-looking output, it can create the illusion that the work is finished. In reality, that output is often only a starting point.
Iteration ensures that raw material becomes something truly valuable.
AI can produce version 0.1 instantly.
Human effort turns it into version 1.0.

The willingness to iterate is one of the most reliable predictors of high-quality work.
Many people abandon projects too early, satisfied with the first workable version. Others continue refining long after the initial idea appears complete.

In an environment where AI can produce ideas instantly, the real advantage belongs to those who continue improving them.
Iteration transforms raw ideas into polished outcomes.
Machines generate possibilities quickly.
Humans transform those possibilities into excellence.

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Many empirical problems involve a “third variable.”
For example:

omitted variables,
mediators,
moderators,
instrumental variables,

all introduce additional variables into an analysis. Yet these variables play fundamentally different causal roles.
One source of confusion is that regression coefficients may change whenever additional variables are introduced into a model. However, coefficient changes alone do not tell us why they changed.
This note clarifies the distinction between:

regression algebra,
causal interpretation,
and causal structure.

The key insight is:

regression algebra explains how coefficients mechanically change, while causal inference explains what those changes actually mean.

title: Post With Code
text:
Why Does Confounding Cause Bias?
Suppose the true model is:
\[
Y = \beta X + \gamma Z + u
\]
where:

(X): education
(Y): wage
(Z): ability

Suppose we omit (Z) and estimate:
\[
Y = \alpha + \tilde{\beta}X + e
\]
Then:
\[
\tilde{\beta}
=
\beta
+
\gamma
\frac{\text{Cov}(X,Z)}
{\text{Var}(X)}
\]
This is the classic omitted variable bias formula.






NoteTechnical Insight



Bias occurs when BOTH conditions hold:

The omitted variable affects the outcome:

\[
\gamma \neq 0
\]

The omitted variable is correlated with the regressor:

\[
\text{Cov}(X,Z) \neq 0
\]
If either condition fails, omitted variable bias disappears.

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Intuition
A confounder acts like a contaminant.
It creates spurious association between \(X\) and \(Y\).
The goal is therefore:

to block the confounding pathway and recover the causal effect.

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
A Simple Mediation Decomposition
Suppose:
\[
M = aX + v
\]
and:
\[
Y = c'X + bM + e
\]
Substituting the first equation into the second:
\[
Y
=
c'X + b(aX + v) + e
\]
which gives:
\[
Y
=
(c' + ab)X + (bv + e)
\]
Thus:
\[
\text{Total Effect}
=
c'
+
ab
\]
where:

\(c'\): direct effect
\(ab\): indirect effect through the mediator








NoteTechnical Insight



In mediation analysis, coefficient changes are not necessarily interpreted as “bias.”
Instead, they may reflect decomposition of the causal effect into:

direct pathways,
and indirect pathways.

title: Post With Code
text:
Marginal Effect Interpretation
Taking the derivative with respect to (X):
\[
\frac{\partial Y}{\partial X}
=
\beta_1 + \beta_3 Z
\]
This means:

the effect of (X) changes depending on the value of (Z).

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Intuition
A moderator acts like a “volume knob.”
It amplifies or weakens the effect.







NoteTechnical Insight



Interaction terms do NOT measure indirect effects.
They measure changing slopes or heterogeneous effects.
Mediation asks:

Through what mechanism?

Moderation asks:

Under what conditions?

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Relevance
The instrument must affect the endogenous variable:
\[
\text{Cov}(W,X) \neq 0
\]

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Exogeneity
The instrument must be unrelated to the error term:
\[
\text{Cov}(W,u) = 0
\]

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
Why IV Works
Suppose:
\[
Y = \beta X + u
\]
The IV estimator can be written as:
\[
\beta_{IV}
=
\frac{\text{Cov}(W,Y)}
{\text{Cov}(W,X)}
\]
Using the structural equation:
\[
\text{Cov}(W,Y)
=
\beta \text{Cov}(W,X)
+
\text{Cov}(W,u)
\]
If the instrument is exogenous:
\[
\text{Cov}(W,u)=0
\]
then:
\[
\beta_{IV}
=
\beta
\]







NoteTechnical Insight



IV estimation isolates the component of variation in \(X\) that is unrelated to the regression error term.
Conceptually, the instrument acts like a quasi-natural experiment.

title: Post With Code
text:
The Standard Confounding Structure
A true confounder is a common cause of both (X) and (Y):
\[
\begin{array}{c}
Z \\
\swarrow \quad \searrow \\
X \rightarrow Y
\end{array}
\]
Example:

(X): education
(Y): wage
(Z): ability

Ability affects:

educational attainment,
and wages directly.

Thus omitting ability biases the estimated effect of education.

title: Post With Code
text:
Case 1 — Mediator
Suppose instead:
\[
X \rightarrow Z \rightarrow Y
\]
Now (Z) is still correlated with both (X) and (Y).
But (Z) is no longer a confounder.
Instead, it is a mediator.
It transmits the effect of (X) onto (Y).
Example:
\[
Education \rightarrow Occupation \rightarrow Wage
\]
Occupation is part of the causal mechanism itself.

title: Post With Code
text:
Case 2 — Collider
Now consider:
\[
X \rightarrow Z \leftarrow Y
\]
Here (Z) is called a collider.
This structure is especially important because conditioning on a collider can create spurious relationships between (X) and (Y), even if they were originally unrelated.
This phenomenon is known as:

collider bias,
or selection bias.

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
What the Formula Says
Bias occurs whenever BOTH conditions hold:

\(Z\) affects \(Y\):

\[
\gamma \neq 0
\]

\(Z\) is correlated with \(X\):

\[
\text{Cov}(X,Z) \neq 0
\]
If either condition fails, omitted variable bias disappears.

title: Confounders, Mediators, Moderators, and IV
text:
A Crucial Observation
Notice something important:

the formula itself says nothing about causal direction.

The formula only depends on:

covariance,
and regression relationships.

At this purely statistical level, regression algebra only “sees” correlation.
It does not know whether:
\[
Z \to X
\]
or:
\[
X \to Z
\]
or whether a meaningful causal interpretation exists at all.







NoteTechnical Insight



The omitted variable bias formula is fundamentally a regression algebra result.
It explains when coefficients mechanically change after omitting a correlated variable.
By itself, however, the formula does not determine whether the omitted variable represents:

confounding,
mediation,
selection,
or some other causal structure.

title: Thailand’s Economic Slowdown: A Case of Structural Drift
text:
8. Any positives?
While the significant structural challenges remain, there would be a “second story” for Thailand—a high-tech reinvention driven by massive global investment and strategic positioning. This is an opportuity for the Thai economy to re-direct its transition from a traditional manufacturing and tourism hub into a critical node for the future digital and electric world.

1. Massive Investment in Digital Infrastructure
Global technology giants are making multi-billion dollar, long-term bets on Thailand’s potential as a digital hub. * Cloud and AI Powerhouse: Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have committed billions of dollars to building cloud and AI infrastructure in the country. * Data Center Hub: These companies are investing in the “invisible infrastructure” of the modern world—servers, cables, and cooling systems—positioning Thailand on the global map for artificial intelligence and cloud services. * TikTok and Regional Data: TikTok’s parent company is also moving forward with a major data hosting project, signaling confidence in Thailand’s strategic regional importance.


2. Strategic “China Plus 1” Positioning
Thailand is becoming a primary beneficiary of the “China Plus 1” strategy, where global companies diversify their supply chains away from overdependence on China. * Experienced Industrial Base: Unlike some neighbors, Thailand already possesses a sophisticated manufacturing ecosystem, industrial land, ports, and a history of supply chain integration. * PCB Manufacturing Boom: The country is attracting major investment in Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs), the essential components for almost all advanced electronics, from phones to medical devices.


3. Transition to an Electric Vehicle (EV) Hub
Although the traditional Japanese-led automotive era is under pressure, Thailand is rapidly pivoting to become a regional leader in EV production. * Chinese EV Investment: Major Chinese manufacturers, including BYD, Great Wall Motor, and GAC Aion, are building factories and expanding their presence in Thailand. * Industrial Preservation: This shift offers Thailand a chance to preserve its identity as the “Detroit of Asia” by trading old internal combustion engine manufacturing for high-tech electric ecosystems.


4. Resilience of the “Bamboo Network”
This is controversial, but a unique source of stability in the Thai economy is the “Bamboo Network”—powerful ethnic Chinese business networks that control over 80% of the country’s largest companies. * Stability in Crisis: These family-run conglomerates (such as CP Group and Central Group) prioritize long-term stability and relationships over short-term gains, allowing them to survive economic crises, coups, and global shifts better than many Western-style corporations. * Modernisation: A younger generation of Western-educated heirs is now pushing these powerful networks toward more transparency and international standards, potentially making the domestic economy more competitive.


5. Existing Strengths and Connectivity
Thailand’s geographic and infrastructural advantages continue to provide a solid foundation for this “rewiring” of the economy: * Strategic Location: It remains centrally connected to mainland Southeast Asia with established highways, ports, and logistics networks. * Large Domestic Market: Despite demographic challenges, Thailand still maintains a large domestic market compared to many of its regional peers.
In summary, a positive outlook for Thailand is defined by its potential to become a strategic digital and high-tech platform for global giants, leveraging its industrial experience to host the industries of the future.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
In computer science, reasoning is typically defined as the capacity for discrete thoughts to build upon one another in order to generate new conclusions — specifically conclusions structured so that an external observer can follow the logic and reproduce the same result.
Historically, one of the benchmark environments for testing this capability was the “blocks world” problem, where an artificial agent had to manipulate objects into a desired configuration.
These early experiments revealed an important threshold:

Once solutions exceeded roughly eight reasoning steps, many early AI systems deteriorated into what researchers described as “reasonable-looking gibberish.”

The systems could imitate logical structure for short chains of thought, but lacked the flexible reasoning required for longer planning horizons.
A modern example of this rigidity appears when Large Language Models (LLMs) are instructed to play tic-tac-toe while intentionally trying to lose. Despite the simplicity of the game, many models fail because they remain trapped in strongly learned patterns (playing to win). This highlights an important insight:

True reasoning requires more than sophisticated pattern mimicry.





Functional reasoning systems generally require two architectural components.








Pillar
Definition
Chess Example




World Model
An internal simulator or representation that predicts environmental changes resulting from specific actions.
The rules of chess and the current spatial arrangement of pieces.


Algorithm
A decision-making procedure that evaluates and selects among possible actions using the world model.
The logic used to determine whether a move improves or worsens the board position.



Historically, AI systems approached this through two major search paradigms.


The system evaluates only the immediate next move and selects the option with the highest short-run value.
For example: - capturing a piece, - gaining material, - or maximizing immediate reward.
This is computationally efficient, but strategically shallow.




At the opposite extreme, the system attempts to evaluate every possible future path.
This quickly becomes computationally impossible.
The chess game tree contains more possible board configurations than there are atoms in the observable universe.





A major transition in AI occurred when researchers shifted away from manually coded heuristics toward neural networks capable of learning environmental intuition through experience.
One landmark example was TD-Gammon in 1989.
TD-Gammon: - used a neural network to evaluate Backgammon positions, - trained through millions of games of self-play, - and improved using reinforcement signals derived from wins and losses.
Remarkably, it achieved near world-class performance using only a shallow one-step look-ahead.




Over time, researchers distinguished between two forms of “intuition.”


The ability to evaluate the quality of a static state.
For example: - estimating the probability of winning from a given chess position.




The ability to predict which moves are promising before explicitly calculating their consequences.
This resembles human instinct: - “This move feels strong.”





In 2014, Clark and Stokeley trained networks directly on human move patterns.
Their architecture: - produced probability distributions over legal moves, - ranked candidate actions according to human tendencies, - and learned stylistic preferences from expert play.
However, these systems plateaued at roughly amateur strength because they lacked a deeper search procedure to validate their intuitive guesses.




The decisive breakthrough came from integrating neural networks with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS).
AlphaGo combined: - policy networks (move intuition), - value networks (position evaluation), - and guided search.
Instead of exhaustively searching the full game tree, the system performed selective simulations (“rollouts”) focused on the most promising continuations.
This allowed computational resources to be concentrated where uncertainty was greatest.




The defining symbolic moment came during Game 2 against Lee Sedol.
AlphaGo played the now-famous Move 37 — a move so statistically improbable by human standards that commentators initially assumed it was a mistake.
Instead, it proved brilliant.
The moment became historically significant because it suggested something deeper:

Machines were no longer merely imitating human strategies.
They were discovering new ones.





Later systems such as AlphaGo Zero removed human training data entirely.
The AI learned solely through self-play.
An important conclusion emerged:

Human examples acted as a “crutch” that constrained exploration.

Pure self-play allowed the system to discover strategic patterns beyond accumulated human tradition.




In 2018, Ha and Schmidhuber introduced the influential paper World Models.
The central idea was radical:

An AI could learn an internal simulator of reality and train inside imagined environments.

The system: - observed the world, - compressed experience into a latent representation, - and then generated simulated futures (“dreams”).
Training no longer required constant interaction with the real environment.
This dramatically reduced the cost of learning.




DeepMind later extended this idea with MuZero.
Unlike earlier systems, MuZero was not given: - the rules of chess, - the rules of Go, - or the rules of Atari games.
Instead, it inferred useful environmental structure directly from reward signals.
MuZero mastered: - Chess, - Go, - Shogi, - and 57 Atari games, without explicit knowledge of the governing rules.




Despite these achievements, a major limitation remained.
Learning one environment did not generalize to another.
A system trained for: - chess, could not automatically transfer its knowledge to: - driving, - robotics, - or language.
Each domain still required retraining from scratch.
This created isolated “skill silos.”




A profound change occurred in 2017 with the paper:

Attention Is All You Need

Originally developed for language translation, the Transformer architecture replaced sequential word processing with a mechanism called attention.
Rather than translating word-by-word, the system learned relationships between words through high-dimensional mathematical associations.
This enabled: - context sensitivity, - long-range dependency tracking, - and scalable representation learning.






Words are broken into numerical units called tokens.
These may represent: - entire words, - partial words, - or punctuation fragments.




Each token is represented as a high-dimensional vector encoding: - semantic meaning, - associations, - grammar, - and contextual relationships.
GPT-2 used vector dimensions around 768.
Modern systems such as GPT-4 operate at vastly larger scales, though exact specifications are proprietary.




LLMs learn through exposure to enormous text corpora.
During training, the model continuously predicts the next token.
For example:

“The dog was barking…”

causes the system to increase associations between: - dog, - barking, - pets, - noise, - and related concepts.
Over billions of examples, the model develops a statistical representation of language.





Modern generative AI is fundamentally:

Prediction at scale.

When prompted with:

“The sky is…”

the model estimates probability distributions over possible continuations.
For example:

Blue → 47%
Clear → 18%
Falling → 12%

The system selects from these distributions.




Creativity emerges when the system intentionally avoids the most probable continuation.
Instead of selecting: - the top prediction,
it samples: - the second, - third, - or lower-ranked possibilities.
This creates outputs that appear: - varied, - surprising, - and human-like.




Importantly, the same mathematical principle extends beyond language.
Generative AI can predict: - the next pixel in an image, - the next frame in a video, - or the next segment of audio.
The underlying mechanism remains statistical continuation prediction.




This capability became practical largely because of Nvidia GPUs.
Originally designed for: - graphics rendering, - and later cryptocurrency mining,
GPUs proved exceptionally efficient at large-scale matrix multiplication.
This allowed modern data centers to compute billions of token relationships in real time.




Recent AI research increasingly resembles the search procedures of earlier game-playing systems.




Prompts such as:

“Let’s think step by step.”

encourage the model to generate explicit intermediate reasoning stages.
This: - decomposes complex tasks, - reduces logical jumps, - and improves performance on reasoning benchmarks.




Tree of Thought extends this further.
Instead of pursuing a single reasoning chain, the system: - explores multiple candidate reasoning branches simultaneously, - evaluates their plausibility, - and prunes unpromising paths.
Conceptually, this resembles Monte Carlo Tree Search applied to language.




OpenAI’s paper:

Let’s Verify Step by Step

introduced reinforcement learning methods that reward valid intermediate reasoning steps.
Rather than evaluating only final answers, the system receives feedback throughout the reasoning process.
This resembles human social learning: - nods of understanding, - expressions of confusion, - approval, - or correction.
Over time, the model learns to: - suppress faulty logic, - and reinforce coherent reasoning patterns.




One major finding of recent research is the relationship between:

thinking time and reasoning quality.

Allowing models to generate more intermediate reasoning tokens often improves accuracy more effectively than simply increasing parameter counts.




To move beyond memorization, researchers increasingly use the ARC Test (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus).
ARC problems require systems to infer: - novel visual patterns, - abstract transformations, - and first-principles rules,
without relying on previously seen internet data.
The benchmark is designed specifically to test genuine generalization.




The field remains divided between two broad perspectives.



This view holds that modern AI systems are fundamentally: - advanced pattern matchers, - sophisticated mimics, - and statistical illusion machines.
According to this perspective: - reasoning chains are not “understanding,” - but only the appearance of understanding.




The opposing position argues:

If a system consistently produces valid reasoning and correct conclusions, the internal mechanism may not matter.

From this perspective: - sufficiently advanced mimicry becomes functionally indistinguishable from understanding.
And if it is indistinguishable in practice:

perhaps it is understanding.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
In computer science, reasoning is typically defined as the capacity for discrete thoughts to build upon one another in order to generate new conclusions — specifically conclusions structured so that an external observer can follow the logic and reproduce the same result.
Historically, one of the benchmark environments for testing this capability was the “blocks world” problem, where an artificial agent had to manipulate objects into a desired configuration.
These early experiments revealed an important threshold:

Once solutions exceeded roughly eight reasoning steps, many early AI systems deteriorated into what researchers described as “reasonable-looking gibberish.”

The systems could imitate logical structure for short chains of thought, but lacked the flexible reasoning required for longer planning horizons.
A modern example of this rigidity appears when Large Language Models (LLMs) are instructed to play tic-tac-toe while intentionally trying to lose. Despite the simplicity of the game, many models fail because they remain trapped in strongly learned patterns (playing to win). This highlights an important insight:

True reasoning requires more than sophisticated pattern mimicry.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
Functional reasoning systems generally require two architectural components.








Pillar
Definition
Chess Example




World Model
An internal simulator or representation that predicts environmental changes resulting from specific actions.
The rules of chess and the current spatial arrangement of pieces.


Algorithm
A decision-making procedure that evaluates and selects among possible actions using the world model.
The logic used to determine whether a move improves or worsens the board position.



Historically, AI systems approached this through two major search paradigms.


The system evaluates only the immediate next move and selects the option with the highest short-run value.
For example: - capturing a piece, - gaining material, - or maximizing immediate reward.
This is computationally efficient, but strategically shallow.




At the opposite extreme, the system attempts to evaluate every possible future path.
This quickly becomes computationally impossible.
The chess game tree contains more possible board configurations than there are atoms in the observable universe.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
A major transition in AI occurred when researchers shifted away from manually coded heuristics toward neural networks capable of learning environmental intuition through experience.
One landmark example was TD-Gammon in 1989.
TD-Gammon: - used a neural network to evaluate Backgammon positions, - trained through millions of games of self-play, - and improved using reinforcement signals derived from wins and losses.
Remarkably, it achieved near world-class performance using only a shallow one-step look-ahead.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
Over time, researchers distinguished between two forms of “intuition.”


The ability to evaluate the quality of a static state.
For example: - estimating the probability of winning from a given chess position.




The ability to predict which moves are promising before explicitly calculating their consequences.
This resembles human instinct: - “This move feels strong.”

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
In 2014, Clark and Stokeley trained networks directly on human move patterns.
Their architecture: - produced probability distributions over legal moves, - ranked candidate actions according to human tendencies, - and learned stylistic preferences from expert play.
However, these systems plateaued at roughly amateur strength because they lacked a deeper search procedure to validate their intuitive guesses.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
The decisive breakthrough came from integrating neural networks with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS).
AlphaGo combined: - policy networks (move intuition), - value networks (position evaluation), - and guided search.
Instead of exhaustively searching the full game tree, the system performed selective simulations (“rollouts”) focused on the most promising continuations.
This allowed computational resources to be concentrated where uncertainty was greatest.

title: Machine Reasoning
text:
The defining symbolic moment came during Game 2 against Lee Sedol.
AlphaGo played the now-famous Move 37 — a move so statistically improbable by human standards that commentators initially assumed it was a mistake.
Instead, it proved brilliant.
The moment became historically significant because it suggested something deeper:

Machines were no longer merely imitating human strategies.
They were discovering new ones.

title: Time-Line of Game Theory
text:
Game theory is the study of strategic interaction — situations in which outcomes depend not only on one’s own choices, but also on the choices of others.
Today, it is used across:
- economics,
- politics,
- military strategy,
- biology,
- computer science,
- artificial intelligence,
- and even cryptocurrency design.
But the road toward modern game theory was surprisingly long.
Its development stretched from:
- ancient legal reasoning,
- to probability theory,
- to Cold War strategy,
- to modern algorithmic systems.
And along the way, it produced some of the most fascinating intellectual stories in modern science.

title: Time-Line of Game Theory
section: The Talmud and the Marriage Contract Problem
text:
The Talmud and the Marriage Contract Problem
One of the earliest proto-game-theoretic discussions appears in the Talmud (roughly 400–500 CE).
The problem concerned:
- how to divide assets among claimants,
- particularly in marriage contracts under bankruptcy-like conditions.
Modern scholars later realized that these discussions resembled concepts from:
- cooperative game theory,
- bargaining,
- and fair division.
In a sense:

Rabbis were thinking about strategic allocation problems over a millennium before formal game theory existed.

title: Time-Line of Game Theory
text:
Fun Fact
Waldegrave’s solution appeared not in a journal article, but in a private letter sent to Pierre-Remond de Montmort.
Game theory was literally born through correspondence between gamblers and mathematicians.

title: Time-Line of Game Theory
text:
Fun Fact: Von Neumann’s Mind
Wikipedia’s description of von Neumann almost sounds fictional.
He made major contributions to:
- quantum mechanics,
- set theory,
- economics,
- computer science,
- hydrodynamics,
- statistics,
- numerical analysis,
- and nuclear weapons research.
He was one of the last true universal mathematicians.

title: Time-Line of Game Theory
text:
Fun Fact: Nash Was Only 21
John Nash wrote his equilibrium paper as a PhD student in his early twenties.
The paper itself was astonishingly short.
One of the most influential ideas in economics emerged from only a few pages.

text:
Another Fun Fact: “That’s Not Nash”
Many people recognize Nash from A Beautiful Mind.
But as the lecture slides humorously note:

“That’s not Nash. That’s Russell Crowe.” :contentReferenceoaicite:5

section: Fun Fact: Shapley Value Is Used in AI Today
text:
Fun Fact: Shapley Value Is Used in AI Today
Modern explainable AI methods use “SHAP values,” directly inspired by Shapley’s cooperative game theory.
Game theory quietly became part of machine learning.

text:
Fun Fact: “Agreeing to Disagree”
Aumann proved a famous theorem:

Rational people with common prior beliefs cannot “agree to disagree.”

If both are perfectly rational and fully informed about each other’s beliefs:
- persistent disagreement should disappear.
Whether this describes real humans is another matter.
